newsitem.title: USA: Calif. Senate paves way for state tobacco suits.
newsitem.headline: Calif. Senate paves way for state tobacco suits.

text.p: California's Senate on Monday approved a bill that would clear the way for the state to sue major tobacco companies to recoup public health-care costs related to smoking.

The bill, by Assembly Speaker Cruz Bustamante, was passed by the Senate on a vote of 29-to-8. The bill cleared the Assembly in April but must return there for another vote because the Senate made minor changes to the measure.
The bill removes any legal barriers to the state attorney general filing suit against tobacco companies to recover state paid medical costs of treating smokers, Bustamante said.
"This bill makes our intent very clear that the attorney general should be engaged in efforts to recover our losses from the tobacco giants," said Bustamante, a Democrat.
"We can't afford to waste any more time while other states push forward with their lawsuits and settlement negotiations. California must be at the table," he said.
Opponents of the bill, mostly Republican lawmakers, had argued the state collects more in taxes from smokers than it spends to treat them for smoking-related illnesses.

California, the most populous state, with billions of dollars in potential claims, has so far not sued major tobacco companies. But pressure has been building on state lawmakers in recent months to join the legal battle.
Republican state Attorney General Dan Lungren has long maintained that a state lawsuit against tobacco companies would likely fail because of a 1987 law shielding them from product liability claims.
Bustamante said his bill would amend that law, allowing Lungren to join other states in suing the tobacco industry.
Bustamante's urgency legislation would, if signed by Republican Gov. Pete Wilson, take effect immediately.
A similar bill by Senator Quentin Kopp, an Independent, was approved by the Senate earlier this year. The Kopp bill is not urgency legislation and would not take effect until 1998.
Lawmakers said both bills could be passed by the legislature and sent to the governor for his signature.
